source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 24): London Session Breakout System with Risk Management and Trailing Stops
instrument: generic/multi (article's default settings reference EURUSD; framework is symbol-agnostic)
original_claim_summary: The article claims that price consolidates in a narrow range in the hours before the London open, and that a decisive break of that pre-session range at/after the London open tends to continue in the breakout direction due to the surge in liquidity and participation.
claimed_mechanism: A directional break of a narrow overnight consolidation range at the London session open reflects a genuine liquidity and volatility shift (new participants entering), so price tends to continue rather than immediately mean-revert.
context: Applies specifically around the London session open, following a defined quiet consolidation window in the hours immediately preceding it.
prerequisite_state: A measurable price range has formed between 03:00 and 08:00 London time, and that range size falls within a configured min/max band (100-300 points default) to exclude abnormally quiet or abnormally wide sessions.
event_sequence: Pre-London range forms (03:00-08:00 London time) -> pending buy-stop/sell-stop orders placed just outside the range boundaries -> price trades through a boundary -> pending order triggers -> position managed toward a fixed risk-reward target with trailing stop.
trigger: Price trades beyond the pre-London high (buy stop) or below the pre-London low (sell stop), each offset by a configurable buffer (10 points default).
invalidation: Price fails to sustain the break and returns through the level before reaching the profit target; fixed stop-loss (500 points default) is hit; or the daily drawdown limit (5% default) halts further entries for the day.
claimed_outcome: The breakout trade runs in the breakout direction to a 1:1 risk-reward target, assisted by a trailing stop (50 points) once a minimum profit threshold (100 points) is reached.
claimed_horizon: Within the London trading session, until take-profit, stop-loss, or trailing stop closes the trade
falsification_condition: If, across many sessions, breakouts of the validated pre-London range revert back through the range boundary before reaching target more often than they continue to target (i.e., no directional edge above random breakout direction), the claim is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 24): London Session Breakout System with Risk Management and Trailing Stops
original_claim_summary: The system only trades pre-London ranges whose size falls between a minimum and maximum threshold, on the claim that ranges outside this band do not represent a tradeable, informative consolidation.
claimed_mechanism: A pre-session range that is too small reflects an illiquid/inactive period with no real consolidation to break, while a range that is too large already reflects a trending or news-driven move rather than a coiled range, so both extremes reduce the reliability of a subsequent breakout.
context: Applied as a pre-trade filter each day before the London session, independent of the breakout direction.
prerequisite_state: Pre-London high/low range has been measured for the current day.
event_sequence: Range measured over 03:00-08:00 London time -> range size compared against min (100 points) and max (300 points) thresholds -> if outside band, no pending orders are placed for that session; if inside band, breakout orders are armed.
trigger: Range width falling within [100, 300] points (default) enables order placement for that session.
invalidation: Range width outside the configured band invalidates the setup for that day entirely (no trade taken).
claimed_outcome: Filtering by range width is claimed to reduce trades taken on non-informative sessions and improve the quality of the remaining breakout signals.
falsification_condition: If sessions with range widths inside the filter band do not show a higher post-breakout continuation rate than sessions with range widths outside the band, the filter provides no real edge and the claim is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 9): Building an Expert Advisor for the Asian Breakout Strategy
original_claim_summary: The Asian session (23:00-03:00 GMT default) forms a low-liquidity consolidation 'box'; a break of that box's high or low as trading transitions into London/NY sessions signals a directional move.
claimed_mechanism: Low overnight participation during the Asian session compresses price into a defined range that functions as a support/resistance zone; when higher-volume London/NY participants arrive, a break of that zone reflects genuine directional interest rather than noise.
context: Applies at the transition from the Asian session into the London/European session, when liquidity and participation step up materially.
prerequisite_state: A completed Asian session high/low box has been recorded (23:00-03:00 GMT default) and current price is confirmed to be trading on the correct side of the 50-period SMA trend filter for the breakout direction being considered.
event_sequence: Asian session box (high/low) forms -> trend filter (50 SMA) confirms directional bias -> pending buy-stop/sell-stop placed just beyond box boundary on the confirmed-bias side -> breakout triggers -> position runs to R:R target or time-based exit.
trigger: Price trades beyond the Asian box high (with price above the 50 SMA) or below the box low (with price below the 50 SMA).
invalidation: Trend filter disagrees with the breakout direction (order not placed on that side); stop-loss outside the box boundary is hit; or the position is force-closed at the time-based exit (13:00 GMT default) regardless of P&L.
claimed_outcome: Breakout trades aligned with the SMA trend filter are claimed to capture the directional move that develops as the London session takes over from the quiet Asian range.
claimed_horizon: From breakout until the 13:00 GMT time-based exit
falsification_condition: If SMA-aligned Asian-box breakouts do not reach their profit target more often than counter-trend or unfiltered breakouts across a large sample of sessions, the trend-filtered breakout mechanism is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 9): Building an Expert Advisor for the Asian Breakout Strategy
original_claim_summary: The strategy forces a flat exit at a fixed clock time (13:00 GMT) regardless of open profit/loss, on the implicit claim that the Asian-breakout edge is confined to the London morning window and decays afterward.
claimed_mechanism: The informational edge from the Asian-range breakout is time-bound to the London session's opening hours; holding beyond that window exposes the trade to unrelated regime/session dynamics (e.g., pre-NY chop) where the original setup no longer applies.
context: Applies to any open Asian-breakout position still active by the designated cutoff time.
prerequisite_state: A position from the Asian-breakout signal is currently open.
event_sequence: Position opened on breakout -> clock reaches 13:00 GMT -> position closed at market regardless of stop/target status.
trigger: Server/session clock reaching 13:00 GMT with a position still open.
invalidation: N/A (this is itself the invalidation/exit rule for the parent setup); the assumption fails if edge persists materially beyond the cutoff.
claimed_outcome: Limiting holding time to the London morning window is claimed to protect gains/limit losses before the setup's rationale (session transition liquidity) expires.
falsification_condition: If trades still open at 13:00 GMT perform, on average, no worse (or better) than a matched sample allowed to run to their original stop/target, the time-based decay assumption is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 9): Building an Expert Advisor for the Asian Breakout Strategy
original_claim_summary: The article claims a 50-period SMA trend filter improves breakout quality by only allowing buy breakouts when price is above the SMA and sell breakouts when price is below it.
claimed_mechanism: Aligning a range breakout with the prevailing intermediate-term trend (as proxied by a moving average) filters out breakouts that occur counter to the dominant order flow, which are more likely to be false/fade rather than continue.
context: Applied at the moment a breakout order would otherwise be armed, as a directional gate.
prerequisite_state: Asian box has formed; current close price position relative to the 50 SMA has been evaluated.
event_sequence: 50 SMA computed -> price location relative to SMA classified as bullish/bearish bias -> only the breakout order matching that bias is placed (the opposite-side order is suppressed or not armed).
trigger: Price above SMA permits only buy-stop arming; price below SMA permits only sell-stop arming.
invalidation: If price is on the 'wrong' side of the SMA for a given breakout direction, that side's order is not placed, regardless of subsequent price action.
claimed_outcome: Trend-aligned breakouts are claimed to have a higher continuation rate than unfiltered breakouts taken in both directions.
falsification_condition: If trend-filtered breakouts do not outperform an otherwise identical unfiltered (both-direction) breakout system on the same data, the SMA-filter mechanism provides no edge and the claim is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 50): Turtle Soup Liquidity Sweeps
original_claim_summary: A prominent N-bar high or low is a known location for resting stop orders; price is often drawn just beyond that level to trigger those stops before snapping back inside the prior range, creating a fadeable reversal.
claimed_mechanism: Liquidity clusters (stop orders) accumulate just beyond well-known swing extremes; a brief penetration beyond the extreme triggers/consumes that liquidity, after which the move loses the order-flow support that drove it and price reverses back into the range.
context: Applies at N-bar extremes that are 'sufficiently old' (i.e., have stood long enough to represent a meaningful accumulated liquidity pool), not at freshly-formed highs/lows.
prerequisite_state: An N-bar high or low reference extreme exists and is older than a configurable minimum age in bars.
event_sequence: Reference extreme (N-bar high/low) established and ages beyond minimum bar count -> price sweeps beyond the extreme by at least a minimum depth -> one or more bars close back inside the level (optionally with a reversal-direction candle body) -> trade entered in the reversal direction.
trigger: Confirmed close(s) back inside the reference level after a qualifying sweep (sell: closes below the swept high; buy: closes above the swept low).
invalidation: Sweep depth below the minimum absolute-point or percent-of-range threshold; confirmation closes that breach back through the reference level; or the reference extreme being too recent (age below minimum).
claimed_outcome: Price snaps back into the prior range after the sweep, allowing a trade with a stop just beyond the sweep extreme and a target at a fixed reward-to-risk multiple or the opposite side of the range.
falsification_condition: If, across a large sample of qualifying sweeps (meeting depth, age, and confirmation-close criteria), price continues beyond the sweep in the breakout direction at least as often as it reverses back through the range, the liquidity-clustering/snap-back claim is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 50): Turtle Soup Liquidity Sweeps
original_claim_summary: A minimum sweep depth, expressed both as absolute points and as a percentage of the lookback range, is required to distinguish a genuine liquidity grab from ordinary noise around the level.
claimed_mechanism: A shallow penetration of a swing extreme is statistically indistinguishable from normal price noise/spread and does not represent a meaningful stop-run; only a penetration exceeding a volatility-scaled depth threshold reliably indicates that resting orders were actually triggered.
context: Applied at the moment price crosses beyond the reference extreme, before confirmation closes are evaluated.
prerequisite_state: Price has crossed beyond the reference extreme by some amount.
event_sequence: Price crosses reference extreme -> penetration depth measured in points and as % of lookback range -> if both thresholds are met, the event qualifies as a candidate sweep and confirmation logic is evaluated; otherwise it is ignored.
trigger: Penetration depth simultaneously exceeding the configured absolute-point and percent-of-range minimums.
invalidation: Penetration depth below either threshold disqualifies the event as a tradeable sweep.
claimed_outcome: Filtering shallow penetrations is claimed to reduce false-positive sweep signals compared to reacting to any break of the extreme.
falsification_condition: If sweep events that meet the depth thresholds are not followed by higher-quality reversals (measured by win rate or R-multiple) than shallow, sub-threshold penetrations, the depth-filter's premise is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 50): Turtle Soup Liquidity Sweeps
original_claim_summary: The reference extreme used for the sweep must be older than a configurable minimum number of bars, on the claim that older highs/lows accumulate more resting liquidity than freshly formed ones.
claimed_mechanism: The longer a swing high/low has stood untested, the more stop and breakout orders are presumed to have accumulated just beyond it, making its eventual sweep a more significant liquidity event than the sweep of a level formed only a few bars earlier.
context: Applied when selecting which swing extreme is eligible to be the 'reference extreme' for sweep detection.
prerequisite_state: A candidate swing high/low has been identified by the N-bar lookback logic.
event_sequence: Candidate extreme identified -> its age in bars since formation is measured -> if age exceeds the configured minimum, it becomes eligible as a reference extreme for sweep/reversal signals.
trigger: Extreme age (in bars) exceeding the minimum age parameter.
invalidation: An extreme younger than the minimum age is not used as a sweep reference, even if later swept.
claimed_outcome: Trading only sweeps of sufficiently 'aged' extremes is claimed to target higher-quality liquidity pools and improve reversal reliability.
falsification_condition: If sweeps of older reference extremes do not produce a higher reversal success rate than sweeps of younger extremes (holding depth/confirmation constant), the age-based liquidity-accumulation claim is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 46): Liquidity Sweep on Break of Structure (BoS)
original_claim_summary: A candle that wicks beyond a prior swing high/low but closes back inside it, in the direction of the established trend, indicates that stops were trapped just before the real directional move, and this combination is used as an entry trigger.
claimed_mechanism: A wick-and-close-back-inside pattern at a known swing point shows that liquidity resting beyond that swing (stop orders) was consumed without the market actually accepting the new extreme, implying the sweep was manipulative rather than the start of a genuine breakout, so the market is expected to reverse toward continuing the prior trend.
context: Applies only when the broader swing structure (sequence of higher-highs/higher-lows or lower-highs/lower-lows) already indicates an established directional trend.
prerequisite_state: Trend state has been classified as bullish (HH/HL sequence) or bearish (LH/LL sequence) via swing-point labeling over a configurable left/right bar window (5/5 default).
event_sequence: Swing points labeled and trend direction established -> price wicks beyond the relevant prior swing low (in an uptrend, sell-side liquidity) or swing high (in a downtrend, buy-side liquidity) -> candle closes back inside on a directional candle body -> market entry taken in the trend direction.
trigger: A candle whose wick breaches the prior swing extreme but whose close is back inside the level, with the candle body directionally aligned with the established trend.
invalidation: Trend state resets to neutral after a trade is taken; a new opposite setup closes existing positions; or price does not close back inside the swept level (in which case no sweep confirmation occurs).
claimed_outcome: Entry after the confirmed sweep-and-reclaim is claimed to capture the resumption of the established trend, with a stop 10 pips beyond the sweep extremum and a 2:1 reward-to-risk target.
falsification_condition: If wick-and-close-back-inside events at swing extremes within an established trend are not followed by trend continuation more often than by further reversal/failure, the trapped-liquidity mechanism is false.

source_title: Automating Trading Strategies in MQL5 (Part 46): Liquidity Sweep on Break of Structure (BoS)
original_claim_summary: A break of structure (a new higher-high in an uptrend or a new lower-low in a downtrend) is used as confirmation that the prevailing trend is still intact, and only sweeps that occur consistent with that confirmed trend direction are considered tradeable.
claimed_mechanism: A fresh structural extreme in the direction of the existing trend confirms that the market is still respecting that trend, so liquidity sweeps that occur against minor counter-swings within that trend are more likely to be stop-hunts before continuation, whereas sweeps that would require abandoning the confirmed trend are not traded.
context: Applies only after a structural break has been detected in the current swing sequence.
prerequisite_state: A sequence of labeled swings (HH/HL or LH/LL) exists, and the most recent swing constitutes a break of structure relative to the prior labeled swing.
event_sequence: Swing sequence tracked -> new swing forms a break of structure (HH in uptrend or LL in downtrend) -> trend direction is (re)confirmed -> subsequent liquidity sweeps are only actioned if they align with this confirmed direction.
trigger: Formation of a new HH (bullish BoS) or LL (bearish BoS) relative to the prior swing.
invalidation: A structural break in the opposite direction resets/reverses the trend classification, at which point previously 'confirmed' directional sweep setups are no longer valid.
claimed_outcome: Gating sweep-based entries behind a structure-break confirmation is claimed to avoid taking sweep reversal trades against the dominant trend.
falsification_condition: If sweep trades gated by a confirmed break-of-structure do not outperform sweep trades taken without regard to structure/trend state, the BoS-gating mechanism provides no edge and the claim is false.

source_title: Grid and martingale: what are they and how to use them?
original_claim_summary: Classic grid trading (adding evenly-spaced buy/sell orders around a starting price) is only profitable in oscillating, range-bound price segments, and fails specifically on strongly trending price segments where price moves persistently in one direction.
claimed_mechanism: A grid's profitability depends on price revisiting levels on both sides of the starting point so that a basket of long and short entries can be closed together at a net-favorable average; a sustained one-directional trend prevents this revisitation, causing the grid to accumulate one-sided losses that a purely price-oscillation-based system cannot recover from.
context: State-based claim about the underlying price path (ranging vs. trending), independent of any money-management/lot-sizing scheme layered on top.
prerequisite_state: A grid of pending buy/sell levels has been placed at fixed spacing (s points) around an initial price.
event_sequence: Grid levels placed around starting price -> price oscillates, triggering multiple buy and sell levels on both sides -> basket reaches an asymmetric profit condition (some filled orders profitable by a configured multiple K over others) -> whole basket closed together for net profit; OR price trends persistently in one direction -> only one side of the grid fills repeatedly -> basket accumulates unrealized loss with no offsetting fills on the other side.
trigger: Asymmetric profit ratio (KClose parameter) reached across the open basket triggers a close; alternatively, sustained one-directional price movement is the trigger for the failure mode.
invalidation: Available margin/deposit becomes insufficient to open the next required grid level, forcing the cycle to remain unfinished and erasing prior cycle profits.
claimed_outcome: In ranging conditions the grid closes basket cycles at a profit; in trending conditions the grid is claimed to accumulate losses that can exceed prior gains.
falsification_condition: If grid baskets deployed during periods independently classified as 'trending' (e.g., by a directional-movement or drift measure) do not show materially worse outcomes than baskets deployed during 'ranging' periods, the range-dependency claim is false.

source_title: Grid and martingale: what are they and how to use them?
original_claim_summary: The article argues that martingale position-sizing (doubling/scaling size after a loss) implicitly assumes a losing streak of a given length is virtually certain to be followed by a win, and that this assumption is mathematically unfounded without an actual directional forecasting edge, making expected payoff zero regardless of the sizing scheme.
claimed_mechanism: Any strategy that only varies position size or order placement in response to past outcomes, without an independent source of directional information, cannot change the underlying win-probability of the next trade; therefore no sizing/spacing scheme (grid or martingale) can convert a fair/negative-edge market process into a positive-expectancy one.
context: General, state-independent mathematical claim about money-management schemes layered on a directionless (or unedged) entry process.
prerequisite_state: A sequence of consecutive losing trades has occurred using a fixed entry rule with no directional edge.
event_sequence: Loss occurs -> next position size increased by factor n relative to accumulated loss -> if the next trade wins, cycle profit covers accumulated losses and lot size resets; if it loses again, size increases further -> cycle repeats until either a win closes the cycle profitably or available margin is exhausted.
trigger: A losing trade triggers the next, larger martingale position.
invalidation: Deposit/margin becomes insufficient to open the next scaled position before a winning trade occurs, causing the cycle (and the account) to fail.
claimed_outcome: Without directional edge, the scheme's expected payoff is mathematically zero (before costs), and in practice ruin risk is claimed to make martingale 'dangerous in any case.'
falsification_condition: If a martingale sizing scheme applied to an entry process with genuinely zero directional edge is shown to produce positive long-run expectancy (net of costs) over a large number of independent cycles, this claim is false.

source_title: Building a Research-Grounded Grid EA in MQL5: Why Most Grid EAs Fail and What Taranto Proved
timeframe: Regime detection on H4; grid spacing derived from D1 ATR
original_claim_summary: Citing Aldo Taranto's PhD research on bi-directional grid-constrained stochastic processes, the article claims grid EA equity variance grows exponentially with time and that a slow, low-volatility directional drift (a 'quiet trend') is the most dangerous scenario because losses accumulate without the counter-moves needed to close winning legs.
claimed_mechanism: When the ratio of price volatility to directional drift (sigma/mu) is low, price advances steadily in one direction without enough two-sided oscillation to trigger offsetting profitable grid legs, so losing legs accumulate roughly in proportion to the drift while variance/risk compounds over time, making indefinite grid operation an almost-sure-ruin process.
context: Applies specifically to bi-directional grid systems operated without a time or drift limit, particularly during low-volatility trending regimes.
prerequisite_state: A grid has been deployed and the market's volatility-to-drift ratio (sigma/mu) is being monitored relative to a minimum threshold (default 5.0).
event_sequence: VolatilityGate computes rolling sigma/mu ratio -> ratio falls below threshold, indicating drift is dominating over volatility (quiet trend) -> new grid level re-arming is paused -> if drift persists, existing one-sided fills accumulate unrealized loss.
trigger: Sigma/mu ratio dropping below the configured minimum (5.0 default) pauses further grid deployment.
invalidation: A change-point-detection (CUSUM) module flags a structural break, forcing a switch out of bi-directional grid mode into a unidirectional trending mode or blocking new deployment entirely; alternatively, an equity drawdown kill-switch forces a full close.
claimed_outcome: Restricting bi-directional grid deployment to periods where volatility dominates drift, combined with forced cycle resets, is claimed to convert the grid's loss accumulation from an unbounded exponential-ruin process into an engineerable, quadratic (triangular-number) loss profile.
falsification_condition: If grids gated to operate only when sigma/mu exceeds the threshold do not show meaningfully lower ruin/large-drawdown rates than ungated grids over matched historical periods, the volatility-gating claim is false.

source_title: Building a Research-Grounded Grid EA in MQL5: Why Most Grid EAs Fail and What Taranto Proved
original_claim_summary: A change-point-detection (frozen-baseline CUSUM) module is used to detect a structural break in price behavior, and firing this detector is treated as evidence that the ranging regime assumed by a bi-directional grid no longer holds.
claimed_mechanism: A statistically significant, sustained shift in price behavior relative to an established baseline (a structural break) indicates the market has transitioned from the ranging regime the grid depends on into a new regime (e.g., a trend), so continuing to add bi-directional grid levels after such a break increases exposure to the exact drift-dominated failure mode the system is designed to avoid.
context: Applied continuously while a grid is active or being considered for deployment.
prerequisite_state: A frozen baseline of prior price/return behavior has been established for CUSUM comparison.
event_sequence: CUSUM statistic accumulates deviation from frozen baseline -> statistic crosses a detection threshold -> change point flagged -> system forced into trending (unidirectional) mode or new grid deployment blocked.
trigger: CUSUM statistic exceeding its structural-break threshold.
invalidation: No structural break detected -> bi-directional grid mode continues to be permitted (subject to the separate volatility-gate condition).
claimed_outcome: Detecting regime shifts before or during grid operation is claimed to prevent the system from continuing to add losing bi-directional exposure into a newly-trending market.
falsification_condition: If grid deployments that continue after a flagged CUSUM change-point perform no worse, on average, than deployments halted at the same point, the change-point-detection mechanism adds no protective value and the claim is false.

source_title: Building a Research-Grounded Grid EA in MQL5: Why Most Grid EAs Fail and What Taranto Proved
original_claim_summary: The EA imposes an unconditional maximum cycle age (72 hours) on any open grid basket, on the claim that variance compounds with time such that a grid basket left open indefinitely will eventually be ruined even if it survives many earlier cycles.
claimed_mechanism: Because equity variance under drift-dominated conditions grows with elapsed time, a hard time limit on any single grid cycle bounds worst-case exposure and forces periodic crystallization of gains/losses, resetting the variance clock before compounding risk reaches ruinous levels.
context: Applies to any currently open grid basket/cycle, regardless of its current profit/loss state.
prerequisite_state: A grid cycle/basket is currently open.
event_sequence: Grid cycle opens -> time elapses -> either a 3% cycle profit target is reached (basket closed, cycle restarts) or the 72-hour age limit is reached first (basket force-closed regardless of P&L) -> new cycle may begin from reset grid levels.
trigger: Elapsed basket age reaching 72 hours, or cumulative basket profit reaching the 3% target, whichever occurs first.
invalidation: N/A (this rule is itself an invalidation/exit mechanism for the parent grid cycle).
claimed_outcome: Bounding cycle duration is claimed to prevent the exponential/compounding variance growth described by the cited research from producing a single catastrophic drawdown.
falsification_condition: If forcing basket closure at 72 hours produces worse risk-adjusted outcomes (e.g., larger realized drawdowns) than allowing baskets to run uncapped over the same historical periods, the time-bounding claim is false.

source_title: Larry Williams Market Secrets (Part 5): Automating the Volatility Breakout Strategy in MQL5
timeframe: D1 (daily bars, entries confirmed on 1-minute closes)
original_claim_summary: When a market has just experienced an unusually wide daily range, that expansion in volatility is claimed to mark the start of a new directional move, so entering in the direction of a breakout defined as a fraction of the prior day's range should capture that new trend.
claimed_mechanism: A large single-day range reflects a genuine shift in participation/momentum (an object 'set in motion'), so price breaking beyond a volatility-scaled threshold from the day's open is more likely to be the start of sustained directional movement than a random fluctuation.
context: Applies daily, using the prior completed day's range as the volatility reference for the current day's breakout thresholds.
prerequisite_state: The previous day's high-low range has been recorded.
event_sequence: Previous day's range measured -> long/short entry levels computed as today's open plus/minus a multiplier times that range -> price closes (on 1-minute bars) beyond the relevant threshold -> position opened in the breakout direction -> managed to a volatility-scaled stop and a reward-multiple target.
trigger: A 1-minute closing price beyond (open + range x buy multiplier) for longs, or beyond (open - range x sell multiplier) for shorts.
invalidation: Price does not close beyond the threshold that day (no trade); or after entry, price reaches the volatility-scaled stop (entry minus/plus range x stop multiplier) before the reward target.
claimed_outcome: The trade is claimed to capture a new directional trend that persists at least until a reward-to-risk target (4x risk default) or the volatility-scaled stop is reached; the article reports an approximate 60% account growth in an 11-month backtest.
claimed_horizon: Intraday to several days, until stop or 4R target hit
falsification_condition: If, on an out-of-sample period, the range-scaled breakout entries do not show a directional continuation rate above what a randomly-timed entry with the same stop/target structure would achieve, the volatility-expansion-precedes-trend claim is false.

source_title: Larry Williams Market Secrets (Part 5): Automating the Volatility Breakout Strategy in MQL5
original_claim_summary: Rather than using a fixed-point breakout distance, entries and stops are scaled to the prior day's actual range, on the claim that this adapts the strategy to the market's current volatility regime instead of over- or under-triggering during quiet or wild periods.
claimed_mechanism: A volatility-scaled (percentage-of-prior-range) threshold automatically widens during high-volatility periods and narrows during low-volatility periods, keeping the breakout trigger's statistical significance roughly constant across changing market conditions, unlike a fixed-point distance which becomes too tight in volatile periods and too loose in quiet ones.
context: Applies across varying volatility regimes for the same instrument over time.
prerequisite_state: Prior day's high-low range is known.
event_sequence: Range measured daily -> breakout/stop distances recomputed each day as a proportion of that day's range -> thresholds shift automatically as volatility expands or contracts.
trigger: N/A (this is a parameterization mechanism rather than a discrete trigger).
invalidation: If realized volatility diverges sharply from the prior day's range intraday (regime shift within the day), the volatility-scaled threshold may be miscalibrated for that session.
claimed_outcome: Volatility-adaptive thresholds are claimed to produce more consistent breakout signal quality across changing market conditions than fixed-point thresholds.
falsification_condition: If a volatility-scaled breakout system does not outperform an otherwise identical fixed-point breakout system across periods of varying realized volatility, the adaptive-threshold claim is false.

source_title: Developing a Volatility Based Breakout System
original_claim_summary: A break of a defined session's high/low is only treated as a genuine breakout if price also clears a separate ATR-based volatility stop set beyond the session boundary; a break of the session level alone, without clearing the volatility stop, is treated as a false breakout to be faded.
claimed_mechanism: A session-range break that lacks sufficient accompanying volatility/momentum (as measured by ATR) is more likely a liquidity probe that will fail and revert, while a break that also clears a wider ATR-based threshold demonstrates enough force to represent a genuine change in market direction.
context: Applied at the boundary of a user-defined intraday trading session window.
prerequisite_state: A session high/low has been tracked for the current active session, and the corresponding ATR-based volatility stop level (session high + ATR x multiplier, or session low - ATR x multiplier) has been computed.
event_sequence: Session window opens -> session high/low tracked -> price crosses the session boundary -> system checks whether price also clears the ATR-based volatility stop beyond that boundary -> if yes, genuine breakout trade taken in the breakout direction; if no, a counter-directional fade trade is taken instead.
trigger: Price crossing the session boundary; direction of the resulting trade (breakout vs. fade) is determined by whether the corresponding ATR-based volatility stop is also cleared.
invalidation: Each breakout/fade signal is only triggered once per session, preventing repeated re-entry on the same session's level; the opposite classification (fade vs. breakout) would apply if the ATR condition is not met.
claimed_outcome: Requiring the ATR-volatility confirmation is claimed to reduce false breakout signals by ensuring trades are entered only when there is sufficient momentum behind the move.
falsification_condition: If session breaks that clear the ATR-volatility stop do not show a materially higher continuation rate than session breaks that do not clear it, the volatility-confirmation mechanism for distinguishing genuine from false breakouts is false.

source_title: Developing a Volatility Based Breakout System
original_claim_summary: When price crosses the session high/low but fails to also clear the ATR-based volatility stop, the system takes a counter-directional 'fade' trade rather than following the break, on the claim that this specific pattern (weak break without volatility confirmation) tends to revert.
claimed_mechanism: A session-boundary break unaccompanied by expanding volatility indicates the move lacks the momentum needed to sustain a new directional trend, so the initial break is more likely a temporary liquidity-driven excursion that reverts back toward the session range.
context: Applied specifically when a session-level break occurs without the accompanying ATR-based volatility threshold being cleared.
prerequisite_state: Price has crossed the session high/low boundary without clearing the corresponding ATR-based volatility stop.
event_sequence: Session boundary crossed -> ATR-volatility stop not cleared -> fade (counter-directional) trade entered -> managed toward its own risk parameters back into the session range.
trigger: Session-boundary cross combined with failure to clear the ATR-based volatility stop.
invalidation: If price subsequently clears the ATR-based volatility stop after the fade trade is entered, the original 'false breakout' classification is contradicted.
claimed_outcome: The fade trade is claimed to profit from the reversion of a break that lacked sufficient volatility/momentum confirmation.
falsification_condition: If fade trades taken on volatility-unconfirmed session breaks do not outperform simply doing nothing (or following the break) on the same signals, the fade-on-weak-break claim is false.

source_title: Meta-Labeling the Classics (Part 3): Filtering and Sizing Bollinger Band Trades
original_claim_summary: A classic Bollinger Band mean-reversion signal (buy when price touches/closes below the lower band, sell when it touches/closes above the upper band) holds in ranging markets but fails systematically -- not randomly -- during trending markets, where band touches instead mark the start of continued moves.
claimed_mechanism: Band-touch signals encode an assumption that price extension beyond a volatility envelope will revert to the mean; this assumption is only valid when the underlying process is range-bound, and when a trend is forming (high ADX with expanding bandwidth) the same band touches instead reflect genuine momentum, so trading them as mean-reversion produces a systematic (regime-driven) cluster of losses rather than random noise.
context: Regime-dependent: holds during low-ADX, range-bound conditions; fails during high-ADX, trend-establishing conditions with expanding bandwidth.
prerequisite_state: Price closes at or beyond one of the Bollinger Bands.
event_sequence: Price closes at/below lower band (or at/above upper band) -> primary model fires a mean-reversion signal (+1 or -1) -> outcome depends on whether the prevailing regime is ranging (reversion tends to occur) or trending (price continues, causing losses).
trigger: Close at or beyond the lower or upper Bollinger Band.
invalidation: Rising bandwidth combined with high ADX at the time of the band touch signals that the ranging assumption no longer holds, invalidating a naive mean-reversion trade on that touch.
claimed_outcome: In ranging regimes, price reverts toward the middle band after a touch; in trending regimes, the same touch signal is claimed to fail in a predictable, regime-driven way rather than randomly.
falsification_condition: If naive band-touch mean-reversion trades taken during independently-classified high-ADX/expanding-bandwidth periods do not lose at a materially higher rate than those taken during low-ADX/contracting-bandwidth periods, the regime-dependent-failure claim is false.

source_title: Meta-Labeling the Classics (Part 3): Filtering and Sizing Bollinger Band Trades
original_claim_summary: A secondary classifier trained on bandwidth-regime and related features can learn to suppress low-quality Bollinger Band touch signals (occurring in trending regimes) while sizing up high-confidence signals, separating the 'which direction' question from the 'whether to trade at all' question.
claimed_mechanism: Because the failure of the mean-reversion signal is systematic and regime-driven rather than random, a model that specifically learns to detect the trending-regime feature signature (notably a bandwidth-regime feature, 'bb_bw_regime') at the time of a band touch can distinguish high-quality reversion opportunities from low-quality trend-continuation traps, and this probability estimate can also be used to scale position size.
context: Applied at the moment a primary Bollinger Band touch signal fires, before a trade is actually placed.
prerequisite_state: A primary mean-reversion signal (band touch) has fired.
event_sequence: Primary signal fires -> secondary (meta-label) classifier evaluates regime features including bandwidth regime -> classifier outputs a probability of the primary signal being correct -> low-confidence signals are suppressed, marginal signals sized down, high-confidence signals sized up.
trigger: Secondary classifier's confidence probability exceeding a threshold at the time of a primary signal.
invalidation: If the bandwidth-regime feature (or the secondary classifier generally) fails to discriminate between eventual winning and losing band-touch signals out of sample, the meta-labeling approach provides no benefit.
claimed_outcome: Filtering and sizing band-touch signals via the secondary classifier is claimed to improve realized performance relative to trading every band touch identically.
falsification_condition: If meta-labeled (filtered and sized) Bollinger Band trades do not show better out-of-sample risk-adjusted performance than an unfiltered baseline that trades every band touch with fixed size, the meta-labeling claim is false.

source_title: Gold Asian Breakout | Buy Trading Robot (Expert Advisor) for MetaTrader 5
timeframe: D1 (recommended); Asian range measured 22:00-05:00 GMT, breakout window London/NY sessions
original_claim_summary: The EA only allows breakout trades in the direction of a higher-timeframe (weekly SMA-100) trend filter -- for example, it will not open sell positions while price is in a weekly uptrend -- on the claim that trading Asian-range breakouts against the dominant higher-timeframe trend produces lower-quality signals.
claimed_mechanism: The weekly SMA-100 is used as a proxy for the dominant multi-week directional bias; breakouts of the shorter-term Asian session range that occur in the same direction as this HTF bias are assumed to have institutional/trend support, while breakouts against it are assumed to be more likely to fail, so counter-HTF-trend breakout signals are suppressed entirely.
context: Applied on XAUUSD specifically, gating every Asian-range breakout signal against the prevailing weekly-SMA-100 trend.
prerequisite_state: Weekly SMA-100 trend direction has been computed; an Asian session high/low range (22:00-05:00 GMT) has formed.
event_sequence: Weekly SMA-100 trend direction established -> Asian range measured -> price breaks Asian range boundary during the London (07:00-11:00 GMT) or New York (13:00-17:00 GMT) window -> trade only opened if breakout direction matches the weekly SMA-100 trend; otherwise the signal is suppressed.
trigger: Asian range breakout occurring in the same direction as the weekly SMA-100 trend, during the London or New York session windows.
invalidation: A breakout occurring against the weekly SMA-100 trend direction is not traded regardless of its own characteristics; additional MA/RSI/spread filters can also veto the signal.
claimed_outcome: Trend-aligned Asian breakouts are marketed as producing the EA's 'highest profit factor' and 'most stable signals, best risk/reward ratio' on the D1 timeframe (marketing figures not independently verified here).
claimed_horizon: Within the London/New York session window following the Asian range
falsification_condition: If Asian-range breakouts traded against the weekly SMA-100 trend do not underperform (in win rate or expectancy) trend-aligned breakouts on out-of-sample XAUUSD data, the HTF-trend-gating claim provides no real edge and is false.

source_title: Gold Asian Breakout | Buy Trading Robot (Expert Advisor) for MetaTrader 5
original_claim_summary: The EA restricts breakout entries to the London (07:00-11:00 GMT) and New York (13:00-17:00 GMT) windows following the Asian range (22:00-05:00 GMT), on the claim that the Asian range only becomes tradeable once the higher-liquidity sessions begin.
claimed_mechanism: The Asian session's low participation allows a range to form, but the range's breakout only carries directional significance once London/New York liquidity providers begin trading, so restricting entries to these specific session windows filters out breakouts that occur during still-thin liquidity and are more likely to be noise.
context: Applied daily on XAUUSD, gating Asian-range breakout signals to specific session-time windows.
prerequisite_state: An Asian session high/low range has formed between 22:00 and 05:00 GMT.
event_sequence: Asian range recorded -> clock enters London (07:00-11:00 GMT) or New York (13:00-17:00 GMT) window -> price breaks the Asian range boundary within this window -> combined with MA/RSI/spread/HTF filters, a trade may be opened; breakouts occurring outside these windows are not actioned.
trigger: A break of the Asian range high/low occurring specifically within the defined London or New York session windows.
invalidation: A range break occurring outside the London/New York windows (e.g., during the Asian session itself or between sessions) is not traded; range validation and spread filters can also block entry.
claimed_outcome: Session-gated breakout entries are marketed as delivering more stable signals than ungated breakout entries, supported by the vendor's claim of '5 years of backtests.'
claimed_horizon: Within the respective London or New York session window
falsification_condition: If Asian-range breakouts occurring outside the London/New York windows perform no worse (win rate/expectancy) than those inside the windows on independent XAUUSD data, the session-gating mechanism is false.
